rv.q: The Big Knife’s first Broadway revival is muscular, moody and stylish, with a mostly solid cast under Doug Hughes’s shrewd direction.

Bobby Cannavale brings a compelling vulnerability to his portrayal of Charlie Castle, the Hollywood star trapped in a corrupt system, while the supporting cast delivers uniformly strong performances in this revival of Clifford Odets' caustic 1949 drama.

This is a mess of a morality melodrama -- overwritten and under-nuanced, wallowing in classic pact-with-the-devil conflict in the style of late-night scandal-sheet noir. And I'm not a bit sorry to have seen it.
Too bad the production only gives us a partial view, a CinemaScope movie seen on a computer screen.
The Big Knife is the kind of play that makes you want to see a movie.
You leave this disappointing production feeling every one of the resulting bruises.
Or, never mind that, to see Richard Kind steal the picture.

Tough-guy movie star Charlie Castle started out as manly but sensitive theater actor Charlie Cass, with big ideals and even bigger ambitions. After 10 years in Hollywood, a succession of simple-minded action movies has made him his studio’s number one box-office draw while increasingly filling him with self-disgust.
Like many a Hollywood creation, “The Big Knife” has a come-hither look it can’t quite make good on.
But all told, Knife doesn't cut as deeply as you might expect it would.
In the Roundabout's rusty redo, the play emerges as a blunt instrument that could have stayed in a drawer.
They do their best to sharpen this Knife, but it’s still got an old, dull blade.
There’s no denying that the Roundabout Theatre Company’s revival of Clifford Odets’ rarely seen 1949 drama “The Big Knife” is misconceived and altogether embarrassing.
The production's star, Bobby Cannavale, dressed in tennis whites or a tuxedo, is not only miscast, but his current hot-stuff career gives the lie to the play's point.

cn.t: Critics find this Odets revival misconceived and sluggish, with a second-tier script that emerges as a blunt instrument despite strong performances. The Hollywood morality tale lacks the energy and bite needed to make its dated melodrama resonate.
